The core idea behind ID is to leverage the anchoring effect, a cognitive bias where initial information disproportionately influences subsequent judgments. ID achieves this by contrasting the logits of the original instruction with those generated from a manipulated, noisy version of the instruction. This contrastive approach aims to guide the model towards generating responses that are more aligned with the intended instruction. The authors propose several methods for creating noisy instructions, including truncating and shuffling the original instruction, providing only input-output pairs, inserting random words, and using an 'opposite' instruction that prompts the model to generate responses that contradict the original intent. Through experiments on various instruction-tuned models and tasks, the authors demonstrate that ID consistently outperforms baseline models, particularly when employing the 'opposite' noisy instruction. The paper also provides a comprehensive analysis of the behavior of ID, showcasing its effectiveness in improving label adherence, coherence, and mitigating imbalances in the decoding process. The empirical findings suggest that ID offers a simple yet effective way to improve the performance of instruction-tuned language models without requiring additional training or fine-tuning. The method's reliance on contrasting logits from original and noisy instructions, inspired by contrastive decoding, presents a unique approach to refining model outputs. The authors' exploration of different noisy instruction variants further contributes to the understanding of how to effectively leverage the anchoring effect in language models. Overall, the paper presents a compelling case for the use of ID as a practical method for enhancing instruction-following in language models, with significant implications for various natural language processing tasks.
